lesson.title: The Vanishing Middlemen: Spotting Reaction Intermediates
lesson.summary: A reaction intermediate is a species that is produced in one elementary step and completely consumed in a later step, so it never shows up in the overall balanced equation even though it is essential to how the reaction actually happens.
lesson.body:
When a mechanism is broken into elementary steps, some species appear that are not present at the very start and are not left over at the very end. These are reaction intermediates: they are created partway through the mechanism and then used up before the sequence finishes, which is exactly why they disappear when you add all the steps together to check the overall equation. In the NO2 plus CO mechanism from the rate-determining step discussion, NO3 is exactly this kind of species. It is produced in the first, slow step, NO2 plus NO2 forming NO3 plus NO, and then it is fully consumed in the second, fast step, NO3 plus CO forming NO2 plus CO2. NO3 never appears in the overall equation NO2 plus CO forming NO plus CO2, yet without it forming and reacting in between, the mechanism would not connect the reactants to the products at all.

It is worth being precise about how an intermediate differs from a catalyst, since both are species that take part in the mechanism but vanish from the overall equation. A catalyst is present at the very start of the mechanism, gets consumed in an early step, and is then regenerated in a later one, so it ends the sequence in the same amount and the same chemical form it began with. An intermediate is the opposite: it is absent at the start, gets created partway through, and is then consumed, so it is never present at either end. A good illustration of both roles appearing in the same short mechanism comes from stratospheric ozone chemistry. Chlorine atoms catalyze the breakdown of ozone through two steps: Cl plus O3 forming ClO plus O2, followed by ClO plus O forming Cl plus O2. Adding these gives the overall reaction O3 plus O forming 2 O2. Here, Cl is the catalyst, since it is consumed in the first step and regenerated in the second, ending up unchanged overall, while ClO is the intermediate, created in the first step and destroyed in the second, never appearing at the start or the end.

Intermediates are frequently reactive, short lived species, things like free radicals, carbocations, or unstable ions, precisely because being unstable is often what lets them react onward quickly in the next step. They usually cannot be isolated in bulk the way a normal reactant or product can, but chemists can sometimes catch them directly, for instance by spectroscopy that detects a short lived species while a reaction is running. When that kind of direct evidence for a proposed intermediate is found, it becomes strong support for the mechanism that predicted it.

This connects back to what you learned about elementary steps and mechanisms in general: the whole point of writing out a mechanism step by step, rather than just the overall equation, is that it reveals species like these that participate in the chemistry without appearing in the net result. Checking that all such intermediates cancel out correctly when the steps are summed, leaving exactly the overall balanced equation, is one of the basic bookkeeping checks used when a proposed mechanism is evaluated.
